speechtext:
Hon. RAYMOND D. MORAND (East Essex) presented the second and final report of the special committee appointed to inquire into and report upon the operations of the commission, under the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act, as amended at the last session of parliament, as follows:
Your committee held twenty (20) sessions and heard thirty-seven (37) witnesses, including five (5) members of parliament, and, after reviewing the evidence, it has been made apparent to your committee that the establishing of national broadcasting in Canada presents many difficulties, for the correction of which time, experience and large expenditure of public money will be necessary.
Your committee therefore recommends:-
(1)	That in view of evidence given before this committee, the government should, during the recess, consider the advisability of amending the act, -with a view to securing better broadcasting facilities throughout the dominion. In the opinion of your committee, radio broadcasting could best be conducted by a general manager.
(2)	That the collection of the fees for radio licences should be simplified and that one licence fee should cover only one receiving set.
(3)	That the provision of the act dealing with advertising should be more liberally interpreted.
(4)	That a greater use of electrical transcriptions be permitted.
(5)	That, pending nationalization of all stations, greater cooperation should be established betw'een privately-owned stations and the commission.
(6)	That chapter 35 of the statutes of Canada for 1933, which expired on the 3rd day of April, 1934. be renewed' until the 31st day of March, 1935.
A copy of the minutes of proceedings and minutes of evidence adduced before your committee, together with papers relative thereto, filed by witnesses, is hereto appended for the information of the house.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
Raymond D. Morand,
Chairman.
Mr. WRIGHT (for Mr. Morand) moved that the report be concurred in.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) asked if the Post Office Department had given any consideration to the issuing of a stamp in commemoration of the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the founding of New Brunswick. During the past two years the department has been dealing with applications for the issuing of commemorative postage stamps in connection with anniversaries in various cities and provinces. Owing to the urgent
Farmers'-Creditors' Act

need for economy and in observance of the regular policy of the department, it has been found impossible to issue stamps except those which would be of nation-wide interest. There are two stamps which will issue on July 1. One is in commemoration of the four hundredth anniversary of the discovery of Canada by Jacques Cartier. The other is in commemoration of the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the settlement in Canada of the United Empire Loyalists. Among the applications received, was one from various persons interested in the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the founding of New Brunswick. The department is aware that this event is not to be confused with the landing of the empire loyalists in New Brunswick, which event I understand was celebrated last year, but it is felt that the new stamp issue undoubtedly will prove of interest in connection with both events. The long established policy of the department has been not to issue stamps in commemoration of provincial or municipal anniversaries, and the issuing of such a stamp as referred to by the hon. member would be a direct departure from this established practice. The two stamps which are now in the course of preparation were considered to be of paramount importance. Widespread demands were received from all parts of Canada that such stamps should be issued and as their issuance would be in accordance with the regular practice of the department, they were given precedence over all other applications. Among other applications the following are mentioned: Toronto Centennial, Trois Rivieres, Diamond Jubilee of British Columbia, Montreal Centennial, Rounding of Basilica at Gaspe, Empire Games at Hamilton, Montreal Harbour Bridge, Welland Ship Canal, Laura Secord Anniversary.

When I asked the question it was not my intention to introduce the subject of celebrating provincial events by the issuing of memorial stamps. The minister has said that it has been against the practice of the department for many years to issue such stamps, memorial stamps being intended to commemorate dominion-wide events.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I did not make the statement to provoke a debate.

I am not going to provoke a debate at all. I merely wish to point out to the minister and the house that the United Empire Loyalists first landed in Canada not in Ontario but in New Brunswick, and that the issue of a memorial stamp commemorative of the 150th anniversary of the event is not dominion but provincial wide.

speechtext:
The amendments made by the
Senate to Bill No. 92 are in one sense important and in another merely a change of words. In subsection (1) of section 3 this house provided for the appointment of one official receiver in each county or district, and the Senate has amended that by providing that the governor in council may appoint an official receiver or receivers in each county or district, and I cannot see that the meaning of it is in any sense changed. The effect of

Dominion Franchise Act
the Senate amendment is to strike out subsection (1) and substitute therefor the following:
(1) The governor in council may appoint an official receiver or receivers in each county or district or for any number of counties or districts of any province to which this act applies, as he may deem necessary or expedient.
I cannot see that there is any great difference in result between the two and I would therefore move that that amendment be concurred in. AVhen we come to section 17 however I have to disagree with the Senate, and I therefore move:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their Honours that this house agrees to their amendment to clause 3 of the Bill No. 92, an act to facilitate compromises and arrangements between farmers and their creditors.
And disagrees to their amendment to clause 17 for the reason that, unless the interest rate is reduced to five per cent after the payment of three months' bonus, there would be no inducement to the lender to accept payment. The purpose and intent of the proposed legislation are to induce the lender, on payment of the principal sum and interest to the date of payment, with the bonus of three months' interest, and thereafter by reducing the interest rate to five per cent, to accept payment without further delay.
And that the clerk of the house do carry the said message to the Senate.
The amendment of the Senate was to leave seven per cent as the amount payable after payment had been made of the principal sum and interest to the date of payment, with the bonus of three months' interest, and there would be little or no inducement, which was the point we were aiming at, on the part of the lender to accept payment. This probably is a misunderstanding of what the purpose of the measure was with respect to that part of the section which is dealt with by the Senate, and I therefore move that we concur in the first amendment and, as regards the second amendment, disagree for the reasons stated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to make a suggestion to the Minister of Justice with
a view solely of expediting the consideration of this measure. Would it be agreeable to the minister that the committee should run through the bill, pass the noncontentious clauses first and hold over the contentious clauses, excepting possibly any minor amendments, and reserve until we get through the noncontentious features any observations of a general nature on the measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite satisfactory to me.

My recollection is
that when this bill was read the second time my right hon. leader took the ground that he supported it with the understanding it was without prejudice to the discussion of any phase of the bill and I want to express my disapproval, on the first clause, the usual time, as I understand the matter, to take exception and strong objection to the principle of a closed list especially as applied to rural areas. We had some experience of that in the past, away back in 1896, in the Northwest Territories and it proved to be utterly impossible to get a proper closed list within any definite time before election day. It lends itself to all kinds of disfranchisement of remote or isolated electors left off the lists and I do not want any more of that so far as rural Saskatchewan is concerned.
Further, in 1912 the Conservative provincial opposition in Saskatchewan of that day led by Mr. McLean, I think it was, took it into their heads right after the election on reciprocity that open lists were bad for their party; that all the frontier areas were usually Liberal and many were obliged to swear on their names on election day. They set up a blockade against the Liberal franchise bill and insisted on a closed list. I do not suppose many in the house are aware of that but for sixty hours in succession the opposition in the legislature of Saskatchewan in 1912 stuck out for a closed list. The government of the day led by the Hon. Walter Scott was opposed to this and warned them what a closed list would mean to them, the imperfect nature of it in a new country like that, but after we had been hanging around the corridors for sixty hours a closed list was accorded them. The election of that year was fought on closed lists, the first time since 1896. The poll on voting day showed that the government were justified in taking the ground that it was the opposition that forced through its views on the franchise bill, no closure existing in those days in the legislature. We had a terrible time getting all eligible voters on the lists and then, although it was the opposition that forced this on the
Dominion Franchise Act

government, the government had to take the responsibility for it. As soon as the election was over, however, we had no more closed lists in Saskatchewan and we have not had since. Of course I realize that is twenty-two years ago and the country is now more settled but the methods of handling closed lists are or may be made just as unfair today, as the government and their officers desire to make them. I must admit quite frankly that after the experience of last year when this government deliberately tried to steal a lot of federal seats in their redistribution bill they will not hesitate to steal the election on election day through this franchise bill.
Order!

There is no order about it; I know what I am saying. It is all very fine for the government to make all kinds of professions of what they desire, but I know what they want. They want political advantage through this bill to their side and I do not want them to get any such unfair advantage. Therefore I am opposed to this provision and whatever clauses it comes up on I desire to give full notice now that I am going to oppose it. The government is not so foolish as to believe that we think this bill is for anybody's manifest advantage but their own.
Moreover,, when I remember the draftsman of this measure and his pedigree and record in the past, one Mr. J. F. or F. J. O'Connor, the same draftsman who drafted the Wartime Elections Act, I am most fearful. It was the most heinous disfranchising act that was ever put on the statute books in Canada. This bill, according to the honeyed words of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, when presenting it, is supposed to be the very opposite of the War-time Elections Act. Honeyed words from the lips but the poison of asps under their tongues is a bad contrast, but that is what it was. Having regard to the before mentioned draftsman of the measure we could not expect anything else. Can a fountain give forth both sweet and bitter waters at the same time?
No.

Can Mr. O'Connor draft an act such as the War-time Elections Act, the like of which we never saw before, and then draft a white man's bill to-day? Certainly not. When the government employed this individual they should have known what would have been expected in the initial draft legislation. Having regard to that fact we should not be quite such simpletons as 
to accept at their face value those nice words with which the resolution was presented, nor can we accept what they are saying to-day that the original draft was in the nature of a memo. I think I have made sufficiently plain that I have a lack of confidence in the government in putting through any kind of franchise act at this time.

Dominion Elections Act

Ever since I can remember
in mountainous municipalities of British Columbia where there are fifteen or twenty polls, available space has been scarce. Residences are on hillsides possibly from two hundred to a thousand feet up, and to reach those separate polling stations it would be necessary to climb the hills. Because of that, for many years back a central polling station has been established in the centre of the town, at the armoury, the city hall or elsewhere, and that procedure continued until the last federal election. I understood at that time it was within the discretion of the returning officer to say whether or not there should be a central polling station, or whether there should be several polling stations. Upon that occasion the federal returning officer much to the inconvenience of the electors determined that there should be several polling stations. For instance, there were fifteen hundred electors, and the new polling stations were scattered all over the hillside. An old man would have to walk up probably five hundred or six hundred feet only to be told that he voted across the gulch, or a woman pushing a baby carriage would go to one station and be told that she voted elsewhere. The result was that officials of the three parties were compelled to send out postcard notices to all electors in the district indicating at precisely what points they should vote. It caused great inconvenience, and was totally at variance with the custom which had been in vogue for many years.

That was exactly the trouble at the last election. There were three parties in the field. Two candidates were keen to follow the old custom of having a central polling station, but the third candidate opposed it. Perhaps I could give my explanation for the information of hon. members. This section states that it shall be a reason for disqualification for any elector to be employed by any candidate. A stenographer, a telephone operator, a worker in a committee room, a driver of a taxicab or automobile, any person employed by any candidate during the period of an election is disqualified from voting. It was pointed out in 1929 in the house or in the committee by the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) that in order to be strictly within the law he was obliged to have the work of checking his polling lists, typewriting and so on done by people from a neighbouring constituency. This provision seems to me to be ridiculous. In these modern days the conduct of an election is something like conducting a large insurance or any sort of business. It is necessary to have twenty-five, thirty or forty people employed in addressing envelopes, sending out circulars, looking after *advertising and taking care of the various activities which must be undertaken by a candidate who hopes to carry on an election with any degree of efficiency. But the fact remains that the candidate renders himself liable to disqualification, and all these other persons are disqualified. This section has been in the act for many years and I think in view of our more enlightened and modern times it ought to be stricken from the act altogether.

I should like to offer an amendment to this clause. Perhaps I might follow the precedent of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and give a general idea of what I have in mind. About a year ago the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) in a speech in this house undertook to tell hon. members that I was very largely responsible for making permissible contributions from corporations and also in speeches across this country he tried to make me more or less directly responsible for the contributions from Beauhamois to the Liberal party.

The hon. member took the lead, the initiative, in the matter. That is what I said.
Dominion Elections Act

The fact is that I suggested an amendment to the Elections Act on May 28, 1930, when that act was up for revision. Section 9 of the act as it then stood read:
No unincorporated company or association and no incorporated company or association other than one incorporated for political purposes alone shall, directly or indirectly, contribute, loan, advance, pay, or promise or offer to pay any money or its equivalent to, or for, or in aid of, any candidate at an election, or to, or for, or in aid of, any political party, committee, or association, or to or for, or in aid of, any company incorporated for political purposes, or to, or for, or in furtherance of, any political purpose whatever, or for the indemnification or reimbursement of any person for moneys so used.
That section had had the effect of prohibiting contributions from labour unions or from farmers' associations to campaign funds. Those contributions were made in the open; they were small in amount but they might very well invalidate an election. On the other hand no provision was made for a report of contributions to central offices. We know there are large campaign funds collected at any general election. Senator McRae said last year that it cost over a million dollars for either of the old parties to carry on a general election campaign. Some years ago the brewers admitted having given large sums to both parties. There is no provision in the clause for any report being made of this central campaign fund, the only provision is for the reporting of sums received by the agent of the local candidate. Apparently then this clause did not fulfil the purpose for which it was designed. Further there were no penalties attached, so it was very largely a dead letter. I did suggest that I had tried in vain to get an amendment exempting the trade unions and other bodies of that kind from the operation of the clause. On an occasion something like this, I did suggest that the clause be struck out. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who *was chairman of the committee said he was quite agreeable; and with no dissenting voice, except, I think one by the Prime Minister on a technicality, the amendment passed. I would suggest that it is hardly fair for the hon. member for Melville to go across the country charging me with exclusive responsibility for having cut out this clause.
Under the circumstances it is only right that some provision should be made with regard to campaign funds, and I make this suggestion, that an amendment of this kind should be added. I am not quite sure that

it covers the ground adequately; I prepared it hurriedly during the luncheon hour:
That section 63, subsection 1 be amended by adding a paragraph, as follows:
(f) a detailed list of all contributions or stocks of literature, posters or other printed material or services supplied from any central committee or any other organization.
As we all know, into most constituencies there come very large supplies of literature from headquarters. Ordinarily there is no accounting made of this. The reports which the hon. member for Charlevoix^Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) speaks about are very different. They certainly make no provision for anything of this kind.
They are no good anyway.

Further than that
there are large quantities of posters and other printed material shipped in from headquarters of which no report is made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be glad to consider .t and also the other suggestion in regard to notification by the returning officer to all persons entitled to vote as to where they are to vote. I am in favour of that, but considering that there are six million names on the voters list it would require an enormous staff throughout Canada to notify them all. They tell we that in ordinary -work a clever stenographer can address fifty postal cards in an hour, which of course cannot be done by penmanship. In eight hours you wtould get only four hundred done. There are twenty-five thousand more names on the list in the ridings, but the total is some six millions. If it were not for the expense I should say yes; but it would be a pretty expensive operation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If there is considerable expense, the alternative lies between the state meeting a legitimate expenditure and placing what is a perfectly proper electoral charge on the shoulders of the candidates and their supporters. The elections act is part of the machinery of government. The elector must know where he is to vote before he can discharge his duty as a voter. It seems to me it should be an obligation of the state to notify him officially where he has to vote.
Where the work is left to committees they have to incur all the additional expense of postage, as well as of stenographic assistance. If the electors were notified by the state, the frank could be used, and all that expense would be saved to candidates and political parties without adding anything in this way of expenditure by the state. Furthermore, it would avoid a great deal of confusion. If a voter received an official card notifying him that he was to vote at such and such a poll, if any question arose as to his being at the wrong poll, the possession of an official card would be prima facie evidence of his being at the right poll. As regards expense, we are at this very moment voting $40,000,000 as a special measure to help to provide labour for the 
unemployed and improve conditions in the country. Of that amount there is over $1,000,000 to be voted for a barracks in the Prime Minister's own constituency. Surely, if we can vote $1,000,000 for a barracks, even should it require $1,000,000 to see that a truly representative poll is taken in a general election, that would be preferable to devoting an equivalent amount of money to the other purpose. I think the bogy of expense is all nonsense, where it is not necessarily considerable and is both necessary and legitimate. I stand for economy, but I recognize that it is absolutely necessary that every elector should know where he has to vote. With closed lists I think he is entitled to be officially informed. At the last provincial election in Ontario I asked my secretary to find out where I was to vote, and he informed me he was obliged to make inquiries from five different sources before he could definitely ascertain where the poll was located. It must be remembered that while some of us may be in the fortunate position of having telephones and motor cars which enable us without too great inconvenience to go from one polling booth to another, the majority of people have neither telephones nor cars, and are without ready means of informing themselves; and, if they are dependent upon what some party committee advises them, they may often be deceived by being deliberately furnished with a wrong notice from some committee. I do think it would relieve candidates and their supporters of a very considerable expense. We are seeking to have elections as free from corruption as possible and to get rid as largely as possible of the necessity of campaign funds. As everyone knows, corruption may arise out of expenses that are essential to the legitimate conduct of elections, and not only out of practices that may in themselves be termed corrupt. Campaign funds have to be acquired for the purpose, and, if we can reduce the amount of campaign funds which are necessary for perfectly legitimate purposes, it will all help in the matter of securing cleaner and better elections. I am glad that the minister agrees with the suggestion and the idea; I believe that members on both sides of the house are practically unanimous with respect to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not want the committee to go away with the idea that this is a new suggestion on the part of the leader of the opposition; it was discussed when he was Prime Minister and was not adopted. We did discuss this very question in the committee

Dominion Elections Act
and the whole committee was in favour of it, the only question being one of expense. I agree that we should do everything to make the franchise as complete and as convenient as possible to the voter, but a line must be drawn somewhere. The next demand will be to carry the voters to the polls. There is a responsibility on the voter to do something for himself. He should take sufficient interest in the question to see that his name is on the list and to poll his vote without being coaxed to do so. I think the suggestion is a good one, and the only thing that causes me to hesitate until I further consider it is the question of expense. If we can overcome that I am heartily in favour of it.

I suggest a compromise. I cannot share the enthusiasm of my leader; I should not like a partisan returning officer to notify the voters in my constituency. It would cost far less to the country if the candidates, within a certain period prior to the election, were permitted to use a frank to send out notices to the electors, and if the electors were not properly notified as to where to go only one or two persons would be to blame, the respective candidates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Suppose a supply of cards, sufficient in number to cover all the names, were given the various candidates and on these cards we printed a frank, "On His Majesty's Service": you would get rid of a large portion of the expense.

That is a good idea. It has been calculated that in large cities like Montreal, indeed in any city, it costs 4 cents per name, including the printing of the card and 2 cents for postage, and that is something worth considering when you run into constituencies of fifty or sixty thousand voters. The suggestion made by the Minister of Justice is an excellent one.
Let us agree on that suggestion.

I should hesitate to accept the suggestion made by the hon. member for Quebec South; it seems to me the suggestion of the leader of the opposition is preferable. There might be trouble if we had a returning officer who was very partisan. The suggestion of the leader of the opposition lifts the matter to a higher level. If you leave it to each of the committees, it means three sets of cards in a great many constituencies, and that is not only a duplication but a triplication of expense all round. Moreover, a procedure of that kind might easily lend itself to manipulation. Someone in any party might
put down a name or an address that was not the proper one and send it out, and the poor elector would have to travel all over the country.
That has been done; there is nothing original about that.

Yes, it has been done and it is possible under the hon. gentleman s suggestion. Very often there is a great deal of confusion as between polling booths in federal, provincial and municipal elections. In the municipal elections in my own city the city clerk sends out a card of notification and it is- found in practice to be helpful. Each elector knows precisely where he has to go and that official intimation helps to clear the situation. I would endorse rather the suggestion of the leader of the opposition; I think his arguments are sound.

Might I point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that there is a wide difference between a notification given in municipal affairs and one given in federal or provincial affairs. So far in municipal affairs, at any rate in most municipalities there are not clearly defined political parties and the municipal clerk is not supposed to be the appointee of one political party. He is as a rule a permanent official who is far above parties. In this case there would be an officer appointed by a party whose duty it would be, if the suggestion of the leader of the opposition is carried out, to notify every elector as to the place where he shall poll his vote. Inevitably, whether a returning officer is impartial, nonpartisan or not, some of those notices and some of those cards will be lost. When a large number of cards of that nature are being distributed, the postmen as a rule are extremely careless with them and a large number will be lost. That will serve to arouse among the people who have not been notified a prejudice against the returning officer and possibly partly against the party which appointed him. I say frankly there is no doubt any man who does not receive his card will say: This is the fault of the party that appointed the returning officer and he is doing it on purpose that I will not be notified. This will only cause ill-feeling and complicate the election issue for no good reason. Were all three parties, if there are three, to proceed to the notification of their electors, surely one out of the three would hit the right man. Time and again in an election campaign complaint is made to me: I did not receive notification from you where the polling place was,

Also, that the managers of the free conference on the part of the Senate will meet in Senate committee room No. 258, at six o'clock, p.m., on this 29th day of June, instant.
A. E. Blount,
Clerk of the Senate.

If this thing is carried on during elections-and it is, there is no use trying to get away from it-at least let us be able to put up a good case before a

judge if we have to go before him, and if the judge is a bit sympathetic and knows that the complaint is not bona fide but only made for the purpose of intimidating a candidate or the person elected, then he will have a chance to throw out any prosecution. That is all we want.

While there may be danger in the clause as it now stands, I submit that to strike it out is a still more dangerous proceeding. There would then be no limit to the amounts that might be spent. It may be that the island of Montreal is an outstanding example of the difficulties of winning an election without a large election fund, but I submit that there are other methods by which elections in that city might be cleaned up than by opening wide the door to a reckless and unlimited expenditure. If this is cut out it will simply be a race to see who can spend the most money, because there will be no limit to what might be done in the way of sending out literature, employing canvassers, having people check and re-check, and so on. That would mean that the man with the deepest purse or the man who could command the utmost in the way of resources would be the man who would win the election, and that is fatal to any real democracy. So I would rather take the chance and insist that if people will not do this work voluntarily they must lose their franchise in that particular election. I think that is the only solution, short of what I suggested several years ago, that legitimate expenses should be put up by the government itself. I think that would be a reasonable proposal. If it is worth while to carry on an election in order to select a government, it seems to me worth while for the country as a whole to put up reasonable expenses. speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I have had some experience in running elections in the city of Montreal, and as a matter of fact I do not employ voters in my own constituency; I employ voters who reside and vote in other constituencies, which is perfectly legitimate. As a matter of fact, if I am to conduct an election in the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George first I must have an inquiry to ascertain that the alleged voter resides where he says he resides. Then I must have some description of him so that he can be identified, and usually in order to identify him by questioning I wish to know his telephone number; if he has an office I wish to know where his office is situated and his office telephone number. I cannot run an election otherwise. In one of my elections a thousand voters were impersonated before they got to the polls. You must have means for a complete identification, and your representatives at the polls must be thoroughly informed so that they may prevent impersonation. At election time I employ people who do not vote in my constituency to do that clerical and protective work.

Dominion Elections Act
You must remember that if you are running an election in the city of Montreal you can go to an association in New York who will supply you with fifty or one hundred or two hundred or three hundred impersonators. These men will come to the city the day before the election, supplied with cards stating whom they are to impersonate; they will go from poll to poll impersonating voter after voter. In one election the only way we succeeded in preventing it was with the aid of a number of young men belonging to athletic clubs, some of them associated with McGill university, who were active supporters of mine. They saw an automobile carrying five or six men; it would stop at one poll and one man would get out and vote; it would go to the next poll and another man would get out and vote; and we then discovered that they were imported persomators. We took the law into our own hands and disabled each one of those automobiles, and defied the police to take charge of us for breaking the law in that way. So we were able to smash the combination. But there must be some way whereby money may be legitimately spent in investigating and informing ourselves with regard to prospective voters, in order to secure such information as will enable us to identify each and preserve his right to vote. I can only avoid the present law by going to some other constituency and engaging men there to do that preventive work for me.

I could not do that.
Your riding is different; I am one of your electors.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There must be some way to ensure that elections will not be carried by impersonation. That is very difficult indeed. So far as I am concerned I will be satisfied if this section remains, but then I may not employ people in my own electoral district to secure the information which is absolutely necessary. In one case I think we secured thirty or forty detectives from another province and some twenty or thirty others elsewhere. Strange to say, before the election I learned that even they were being bribed. We brought some sixty of them into the main committee room, told them we knew they were being bribed and were working for the opposite party and asked those who admitted it to take two paces to the front. Two-thirds of those men took two paces to the front, admitting that they were working for the other party and not for us. Such a situation is difficult but some way must be found to remedy it. I have evidence that at least fifty or sixty blank warrants were issued for use in my constituency. They were signed
by a judge to be filled out when necessary. One committee in the St. Lawrence ward of my constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George, composed of respectable men, were arrested and put in gaol before the poll opened, through the use of blank warrants ostensibly signed by a judge in the city of Montreal.
I have had police officers come to my main committee room where most representative women of the city were engaged on the telephones to persuade the voters to come to the polls. Those police officers had blank warrants which had been filled out on the street, with which they attempted to come in and arrest the most representative people in the city. We have stood at the door and said we would use strong measures if they attempted to carry these warrants into effect, because we knew they were false and fraudulent. That sort of thing is carried on, and it is not surprising to find that in the constituency of St. Lawrence-St. George the election expenses have run up as high as $120,000 or $125,000 in a single election. I know of one case where the candidate contesting the election spent $75,000, and there was a contribution of $25,000 to the election fund which had never been reported to him.
I claim no special purity whatsoever, but I do claim that I have taken every possible step to prevent fraud. No dollar has been expended except on * the approval of an auditor, and every person who works for me during an election is told that we have put up a fund to send him to gaol if when working in my interests he secures a vote for me by fraudulent means. I have done all I can, and there it remains.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let us get this thing straight. Do I understand that objection is being taken to section 63 by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) and to sections 73 and 74 by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power)? Are these agreed to?

That statement has been made on the floor of the house and I want to contradict it. On section 46-Manner of voting.

Mr. Chairman, I desire to move an amendment to section 46. I understand that the act which we are amending is an instrument to assist in the carrying out of the will of the electorate in electing members
of the House of Commons. I understand that the underlying principle is that the House of Commons shall truly represent the will of the people so voting. I think hon. members will agree with me when I say that it would be rather an accident if under the system of electing which we have been considering in this bill we should return to parliament a true representation of the will of the people. I do not think it is necessary for me to enter into any exhaustive treatise on the subject of proportional representation. This has been put forward from time to time in this house as a remedy for the fact that very often after an election the will of the majority of the people has been defeated by the method of elections. Fortunately, proportional representation is not a new thing in this house. It has been discussed exhaustively on several occasions. I would refer hon. members to the discussion which took place in this house in 1921, I think on the motion of Mr. Sexsmith. I refer them also to the committee of the house which was appointed to investigate the whole matter as a result of that motion. I also refer them to the motion made by Mr. W. C. Good on May 10, 1922, when this matter was covered both comprehensively and in detail. As the principle of proportional representation is well understood by hon. members, I shall not attempt anything more at this time than to state the important points which now concern us in view of the fact that the Elections Act is now before us.
I should like to draw attention to the weaknesses of the present method of voting. I think the first thing every hon. member should do is to face frankly the weaknesses in the present voting system and for which proportional representation is the proposed remedy. As I have said, it would be accidental if the present system of voting resulted in a parliamentary membership which reflected the true will of the people. Under the present voting system it is possible for a minority to be either entirely excluded or to have a representation far below that to which their voting strength properly entitles them. On the other hand, it is possible for a minority to obtain representation in parliament far in excess of that which is warranted by their voting strength. One or the other of these undesirable results occurs to varying degrees in every election. In some elections a party representing a minority of the electorate goes into power, thus depriving the party receiving the majority of the votes from forming the government, as it should do properly. An occurrence of that sort certainly violates the true principle of representative government. In
Dominion Elections Act

other cases a large majority may have no representation at all, as occurred in the recent election in Saskatchewan where the Conservative party, having roughly over one-third of the entire votes of the province, did not secure a single representative. The recent elections in British Columbia and Ontario demonstrate the same weaknesses in our voting system, to which I have referred already. I mention these elections because they are fresh in our memories and we can refer to the facts very easily. An examination of the results of almost any election conducted under the present system of marking ballots would give similar evidence.
I refer to two other instances. In the dominion elections of 1926 the Conservative party polled 83,000 more votes than the Liberals, yet had 25 fewer seats. In the federal elections of 1930 the Conservatives polled 1,909.955 votes and obtained 136 seats while all other parties polled 1,989,040 votes and obtained only 107 seats. Under proportional representation the Conservatives would have had 119 seats and the other parties in the house a total number of 124 seats. This makes a difference of 17 seats which the Conservatives obtained under an unjust system of voting. An examination of the figures of almost any election will reveal that it is practically impossible under the system in vogue to procure a parliamentary membership which reflects accurately the opinion of the voters. In other words, we have what the Right Honourable David Lloyd George called an "anomalous, unjust and grotesque electoral system which is a fraud and a mockery of democracy." So much for the defects of the present system of voting.
Proportional representation is a method .of voting which gives representation of citizens on elected bodies in proportion to their voting strength, thus ensuring that the majority of the electors shall rule, while at the same time providing .that all considerable minorities shall be heard. The method of voting adopted under proportional representation is called the "single transferable vote." This implies:
1. That constituencies shall be grouped or be made large enough for the purpose of electing several members, the number to be fixed according to what is practically convenient.
2.	That while there are several members to be eleoted in such a grouped constituency, each elector shall have, as now, only one vote.
3.	The elector, in marking his ballot, will use the figures 1, 2, 3, and so on, indicating the order of his preference of the candidates, instead of marking an "X" opposite only one of the candidates, as he now does. Voting

is quite as simple for the elector under proportional representation as it is under the present system, the only difference being in the task of the returning officer in making the count and in the results of the election which a true voting system would yield.
4.	The vote of an . elector may be transferred according to the choice as indicated by him in marking his ballot.
5.	A vote may be thus transferred according to indicated choice in the event of the candidate against whose name the figure (1) has been put not requiring to use the vote thus given. There are two conditions under which the candidate of the first choice may not require the vote of an elector. These are:
(a)	if he is hopelessly defeated; or (b) if he has a number of first choices equal to or greater than the required majority.
In the former case the candidate so hopelessly defeated is dropped, and the second choice attains the status of the first choice, and so on until each ballot is exhausted in the election of a candidate, whereas in the case of the single transferable vote in multimember constituencies, the surplus above the desired majority may be transferred in the order of the indicated choice, as well as the votes giving first choice to a candidate who comes last in the running.
6.	The majority required in a grouped constituency is determined on the same principle on which a majority is determined in a single member constituency. That is to say, a majority in a single member constituency is determined by dividing the total number of votes by one more than the members to be elected and adding one. If there were five members to be elected, the total vote would be divided by six, and adding one to that quotient would give the majority required by each candidate, or as it is called, the quota.
7.	In single member constituencies this principle of vote transference is known as the alternative vote. It is applied only when there are more than two candidates running in a single member constituency, and it ensures that the elected member shall obtain a majority of the votes cast in the constituency. The candidate with the lowest number of votes in this case is dropped, and his votes are transferred to the others according to the choice indicated by the voter. In this way the candidate elected will finally obtain a true majority of the votes cast in the riding. While the alternative vote does give a majority in each riding to the elected member, it would not in itself prevent the total membership of the house representing a minority vote, nor would it be a guarantee that minorities would have representation. It

Dominion Elections Act
only guarantees a majority in each riding where it is used.
The transfer of votes according to choice may be carried out with complete justice to each candidate and to the electors concerned. The method may be illustrated in the following manner. Let us say that the quota required to elect a member in a grouped constituency is 2,000. A obtains
3.000.	He therefore has 1,000 votes that are useless to him. One thousand votes happens to be a third of all the votes which were marked with a "1" for him. The returning officer, therefore, goes over the three thousand ballot papers a second time, and discovers the names against which the second choice have been marked. Let us assume that candidate B is second choice on 2,400 ballots and candidate C is marked second on 600 papers. We have seen that candidate A can spare one-third of all his 3,000 votes. He can, therefore, spare to B one-third of 2,400 of the ballot papers on which B is marked second choice, or 800. He can also spare to C one-third of the 600 on which C is second choice, or 200. This would result in electing A with his proper majority of
2.000,	and would transfer the other thousand to B and C proportionate to the choices indicated, which as we have seen was 800 votes to B and 200 to C.
Is proportional representation the remedy? That proportional representation would do as it claims it would do, namely, result in an elected assembly which correctly reflected the opinions of the voters concerned, there can be no doubt. Fortunately, the system is used in many countries, and in many cases other than in elected public bodies. I quote only one case. The provincial election in Alberta in 1930 gives us a notable example. Proportional representation is applied in the cities of that province. I quote what happened in the city of Calgary in the 1930 election. The Conservatives obtained, in the final count, 10,519 votes. They elected three members. The Liberals obtained 7,082 votes. They elected two members. Labour obtained 3,492 votes, and elected one member. Contrast these figures with rural ridings in Alberta at the same election, when the U.F.A., with a vote of 70,957 elected thirty-four members. The Liberals, with 34,187 elected eight, the Independents with 23,832 elected three, and the Conservatives with 7,481 elected none, while Labour with 6,156 elected two members. The figures should have been, under proportional representation, 24 instead of 34 U.F.A., 11 instead of 8 for the Liberals, 8 instead of 3 for the Independents, and 2 instead of none for the Conservatives.

Dominion Elections Act

I have taken a little time outlining proportional representation, because I want to make it clear that while the amendment which I shall move does not include that method, in my opinion until that system is applied we shall not get rid of the whole difficulty to which I have alluded, namely, that under the system now used minorities may come into power while on the other hand they may not have representation at all-results depending on the accident as to how the votes happen to be divided in constituencies where more than two candidates run.
How would the hon. member prevent plumping under that system? Suppose there were three candidates, how would you make sure that they indicated first, second and third choice?

There is no possibility of preventing the voter from doing what he pleases; he may exercise all his choices or only one. If he decides to use only one, there is no discrepancy or injustice done him at all; he has done all that he wanted to do, and that is often done. In many cases voters do not use all their preferences, but in most instances they do, and with satisfactory results.
I am glad to say that in urging the adoption of the alternative vote in single member constituencies where more than two candidates are running, I am able to quote the recommendation of a special committee appointed by this house in 1921, and which committee reported to the house on the 13th of May that same year in part as follows:
It must be apparent to all that the present system of election in single member constituencies meets fully the purpose intended only when not more than two candidates are nominated. Rpcent experiences in elections in Canada have brought home to our people the fact that where three or more candidates present themselves in single member constituencies, the candidate declared elected may and often does, represent merely a minority of those voting in the constituency.
Your committee believes that in constituencies where more than two candidates present themselves, the adoption of the alternative vote offers a solution of the difficulty, inasmuch by such method the candidate finally declared elected would represent the choice of the majority of the electors.
The system of the alternative vote has its application only in those constituencies in which more than two candidates present themselves. The work of the elector is simple. Instead of marking a cross opposite the name for which he desires his vote to count his privilege is to place the figures 1 and 2 after the names of his first and second choices. If upon the counting of the ballots it is found that a majority of those voting have placed the figure one (1) after the name of one of

the candidates, then that candidate is declared elected. Should, however, it be found that none of the candidates has received an absolute majority, then in such event the following procedure is adopted. The candidate having the lowest number of first choices is dropped and the second choices expressed on his voting papers are transferred to those indicated on such ballots. This procedure of dropping the candidate having the lowest number of votes after each count is continued until but two candidates remain, and the candidate who has the greater .number of votes of these two is declared elected.
Your committee is of the opinion that this system will give a truer reflection of the desires of the voters in the various constituencies than will be obtained where more than two candidates run under our present method of counting the votes.
As already stated, the only difference to the voter in marking his ballot is that he uses figures instead of an "X" or a cross. In actual practice it has been shown that this method of marking ballots is as simple to the electors as the other, and the percentage of ballots spoiled in provinces where this system is used is no greater than that of those that used to be spoiled under the old system.
May I, in further urging the adoption of the alternative vote in one-member constituencies where more than two candidates are running, draw the attention of the committee to the figures in a recent election, which figures, I think, will give point to the contention. Again referring to the election in Saskatchewan we find that the Liberals obtained 173,066 votes and secured forty-nine seats; the Conservatives polled 103,647 votes and got no seats at all; the Farmer-Labour party polled 87,709 votes and got five seats. In other words, the Conservatives and the C.C.F. combined had a plurality of 18,290 votes and elected only five members, while the Liberals, who were in an actual minority of the votes polled in that province, secured forty-nine seats. If the object of the election act is actually to assist the people of this country to say who shall govern, the method of voting must be altered. Of course I am not arguing that if we had had the single alternative vote in Saskatchewan the result would not have been the same ; the electors might have voted Liberal on second or third choice, but they should have had the privilege; that is all I am contending. I am sure all hon. members will agree with me it is our duty to give the electorate that opportunity to make a second choice in cases where there are three or more candidates running in one-member constituencies so that the individual who may be elected will have a majority of the votes in that riding.

Dominion Elections Act
I would gladly have moved the acceptation of the entire proportional representation proposal, but I know, in order to put that into effect, we have to group our constituencies in some form or another and that would mean going over the whole redistribution again. At this time of the session, and probably for all I know, the last session and perhaps the last parliament for some, it is better, I think, that we should confine the amendment to the alternative vote which is practicable and which would go some way at least toward remedying the evil. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer):
That section 46 be amended by striking out subsection 3 and substituting therefor the following:
Every voter shall have one vote only which may be transferable in the manner hereinafter provided.
The voter on receiving his ballot paper shall forthwith proceed into one of the compartments of the polling place and there mark his ballot paper with the black lead pencil provided, as follows:
(a)	Shall place the figure 1 on the ballot paper within the white space containing the name of the candidate who is his first choice and every vote given by placing the said figure 1 in such white space shall be a "first preference vote."
(b)	May in addition to the figure 1 authorized by this section place on his ballot paper the figure 2 within the white space containing the name of his second choice, the figure 3 within the white space containing the name of his third choice and so on in the order of the candidates he would prefer if the candidate of his prior choice does not need his vote, or cannot be elected. He may thus express as many choices as there are candidates.
(c)	He shall then fold the ballot paper so that the initials and stamp on the back of it and the number on the counterfoil can be seen without opening it and hand it to the deputy returning officer, who shall without unfolding it ascertain by examining his initials and the stamp and the number of the counterfoil that it is the same ballot paper that he furnished to the voter and shall then in full view of all present including the voter, remove the counterfoil and tear up or otherwise destroy it and place the ballot paper in the ballot box.
This amendment has been taken verbatim from the Alberta Elections Act which provides for this method of voting, and in the event of the committee carrying this amendment there are several other clauses that would have to be correspondingly amended. For instance, the clause dealing with spoiled ballots would have to be amended; the instructions to the returning officer would have to be slightly amended, and the facsimile of the ballot would have to be slightly changed, but beyond that very few changes would have to be made. I suggest that if the committee did feel like accepting this, we could avail
ourselves of the Alberta Elections Act and if it did not suit us in its entirety, it would at least form a basis for the amendments necessary.
I conclude by making an appeal to the leaders on both sides of the house to call off the whips in connection with this vote. Recognizing that there is a wrong here and in a matter of this sort, taking all things into consideration, the leaders of the house might very well allow hon. members to settle this question as they themselves actually think outside all party considerations whatsoever. If under those conditions it is defeated I shall be, not content but at least I shall know that we have acted according to what we actually think individually. I suggest that the leaders take that suggestion into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sure the committee appreciates the very able and concise manner in which the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) has presented the question not only of proportional representation but also of the alternative vote. I had noticed that my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin was going to present this matter by way of amendment during the committee stage of this bill; he mentioned the matter in the committee but the committee thought it would not be well to consider it there and that it should be discussed in committee of the whole.
I hope he will not think me disrespectful if I do not seek to elaborate what may be called the case against proportional representation and the alternative vote. I am well aware that there are certain sections of the country and large bodies of people who are entirely favourable to a change in our electoral system by the adoption of some means akin to the suggestion which the hon. member has just made, but I do not think there is in Canada any very general demand for a change. I would not be prepared to say that there is not a great deal of merit in the proposal, but I do not think that at this time in the history of the country and at this hour of the present session it would be profitable to enter upon a prolonged discussion of this subject. I think it would be better if my hon. friend were content to let the matter lie until a later date, after another general election. I do not think that the present time is opportune for the consideration of a question of this kind, therefore I must tell my hon. friend that at present we cannot look favourably upon the proposed amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I have already supported the principle of the alter-
Dominion Elections Act

native vote in this house and I feel that I am bound to support the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Irvine) although I agree to some extent with what my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) says as to the lateness in the present session and the difficulty of considering on its merits at this time a question which involves such an important change in the election law of the country. I only regret that this matter had not been brought before the house at an earlier stage of the session. I must call the attention of the committee to the fact that this House of Commons has already expressed itself as being in favour of the principle of the alternative vote, not only by a vote in the house in 1923 but also through the report of a committee in 1921 which had been sitting for a long time and which recommended the adoption of the alternative vote, a report which was accepted by the house. I might say that in Ontario also during the session of 1921 a committee reported favourably on the principle of the alternative vote.
There is all the difference in the world between the alternative vote and proportional representation. Under the system of proportional representation minorities are represented in parliament. The alternative vote is the opposite of that; it is to assure the representation of the majority at all times. In England a royal commission investigated that matter for a long time and declared against the adoption of the proportional representation system but in favour of the alternative vote. Their report was accepted by the House of Commons by a majority of one. but the Lords rejected it. It was revived later, in 1924, I believe, when the Labour government was in office. Mr. Henderson for the government said that if it were limited to the alternative vote they might adopt it, but the motion was for proportional representation as well. The Liberal party in Great Britain at every annual meeting adopts a resolution in favour of both proportional representation and the alternative vote, but I must say that the Labour party in England seem to have changed their views when they came into power and refused to put into effect what they had been advocating in opposition.
There is no doubt that the alternative vote system is a fair way of assuring representation of the majority in each constituency in the House of Commons. In many continental countries they have what they call the ballottage-I do not know whether "ballot-tage" would be a good translation-meaning that when no candidate has the absolute majority of the votes the weakest candidates are eliminated, and eight days after the date

of the general election they hold a special election between the two strongest candidates. It is the same thing except that it happens after the election while under the alternative vote it happens at the time of the election.
I think there is more justice in that system than in our present system of electing the one who in the polling comes first. There are electors who would prefer one candidate on account of certain planks in his platform, but would like another on account of certain planks, in his. Nobody is perfect, and there are always various questions submitted to the electors; it is a good thing that the electors give their first vote to the candidate they prefer, but have a chance to make a second selection. In the end it ensures that no member of the House of Commons would be there against the will of the majority of the electors in that constituency. I repeat that I think this is a fair method which should be accepted in this country. I am not quite sure, however, that at this late hour of the session, when no educational work has been carried on and when the question has not been submitted to a committee, as should be done before such a radical change is effected, it is wise to press the amendment. I quite understand that there are those who would not be willing to vote favourably under these circumstances, but so far as I am concerned I will support the amendment of my hon. friend.

I should like to give my support to the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine). I do not see that there can be any reasonable objection advanced to the alternative ballot, though there are objections to proportional representation in a country like Canada. Our population is too scattered; it would necessitate very large constituencies, and for these reasons to my mind proportional representation in Canada is impracticable. But as I see it there can be no objection to the alternative vote. I do not think the objection that it is late in the session and that the system is not sufficiently well known should carry weight. This is not a new system in Canada. We have had it for some years in Manitoba; I think it was introduced by the Liberal government about 1920 or thereabouts. I think I am correct in saying that three provincial elections have been held under the system. In Manitoba we have both proportional representation and the alternative vote. In the city of Winnipeg we have proportional representation; Winnipeg elects ten members. In the last provincial election the Liberal-Progressive government elected three who passes the pole first. There are electors

members, the Conservatives elected three, and the Independent Labour party elected four. I think it was pretty generally conceded that this was a fair representation of the wishes of the electors. In the great majority of the constituencies the Liberals and the Brackenites, as they are sometimes called, formed a coalition, and in most constituencies there were only two candidates. There were, however, some three or four constituencies-I have forgotten the exact number-in which the result depended upon the second choice of those who had voted for candidates who were eliminated by virtue of being out of the running entirely, but I think when the second count was made the candidate previously receiving the majority of the votes was elected, which expressed the wishes of the people. I think in every case it happened that the candidate having the largest number of votes also received the majority of the second choices, but it might have been the other way just as easily.
I do not think we should have a condition such as resulted in Saskatchewan after the last provincial election. The probability is that if the alternative ballot had been used in that province the C.C.F. would have been eliminated completely and a number of Conservatives would have been elected; at least that is possible. Whether or not it would have been desirable, of course, is a matter of opinion. However, I do not think it well that large bodies of the electorate should have no representation in the house. I have been a supporter of the alternative ballot for the last twenty years, or ever since it was brought to the attention of the people, and I should like to give my support to the amendment that has been moved. I do not think the objections that have been raised are valid, in view of the fact that it is such a simple matter. It is not as though we were bringing in some elaborate scheme; this is so simple that we might as well pronounce upon it now as at any other time. It is simply doing in one operation what in our nominating conventions we do in two. If three candidates are nominated the low man drops out and a second vote is taken, giving those who voted for that man an opportunity to exercise a second choice as between the two candidates remaining. That is all it amounts to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE SMALL LOAN COMPANY OP CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since
yesterday, when we dealt with the amendment to the Loan Companies Act, I have given some consideration to the preparation of new sections for the amending bill, No. 123. The proposal is at this session to make all companies heretofore or now or hereafter incorporated subject to the amending bill or, as it will be, the amending act. Section 111 of the Loan Companies Act will read as follows:
Where it is established to the satisfaction of the Minister of Finance that any company has, subsequent to the passing of this act, in respect of any loan or other transaction, charged, imposed or collected, directly or indirectly, interest and other charges, of any kind, nature or description whatsoever, exclusive of fees imposed for registration purposes,-
That probably should be changed to "disbursements imposed for registration purposes," as suggested by the hon. member for Battle River this morning.
-amounting in the aggregate to more than two per centum per month on the monthly balance due by the borrower-
And I suggest that it should be "owing by the borrower."
-the minister may recommend to the governor in council that the charter of the company be forfeited, if it be a dominion company, and that its dominion powers be terminated if it be other than a dominion company, whereupon the governor in council may by order provide that upon such day as may thereby be fixed,
(a)	if the company be incorporated by an act of the parliament of Canada, its charter shall be forfeited;
(b)	if the company be otherwise incorporated, any or all rights, powers, franchises or authorities granted to it by any act of the parliament of Canada shall cease and determine.
2. Upon the making of any such order, such charter shall be forfeited or such rights, powers, franchises or authorities shall be terminated, according to its terms, as fully and effectually as if the provisions of _ such order in council were incorporated in this act.
Bill 123 has been reprinted and now appears on the files of hon. members. Since

yesterday I had the opportunity to look into the Money Lenders Act of Great Britain which was passed in 1927, and about which it will be remembered a very great deal of discussion took place both in the Lords and in the Commons. Also I have had an opportunity briefly to study the provisions of American statutes dealing with money lenders. In Great Britain the maximum is four per cent per month, by statute. That covers all charges such as we have here. In many of the American states the rate runs between three per cent and four per cent. As I indicated to members of the committee my own view is that two per cent may be too small, and that two and a half per cent would seem to be the minimum we might hope to use in this country, having regard to the experience of other countries.
Frankly I may say I have no idea that these small companies discharged the useful functions in all countries which an investigation by the Russell Sage Foundation disclosed. As they are the subject matter of much legislation in various countries my own view is that the enactment of this amendment will protect the public in the meantime, and that we could pass at next session of parliament a money lenders' act modelled along the general principle of the British legislation. For instance, it was news to me that one company on the American continent has about four hundred agencies, and does a very substantial business with a limitation much greater than that which is imposed here. I believe it operates at a rate of three and a half per cent.
Under the circumstances I desire to assure the hon. member for Macleod that it is my intention to proceed with this bill immediately the opportunity offers, and to make all companies, which heretofore have been, are being or may hereafter be incorporated, subject to it. The limitation mentioned in the bill is two per cent, but after reading the British Moneylenders Act, and other legislation, I may say that when the time comes we may adopt a rate of two and a half per cent instead of two per cent.

speechtext: Mr. G. G. COOTE (Macleod) moved the second reading of Bill No. 122, to amend the Interest Act.
Explain.

This bill asks that no interest exceeding the rate or percentage of five per cent per annum shall be chargeable, payable or recoverable on the whole or any
Interest Act-Mr. Coote

part of the principal money advanced on or secured by mortgage of real estate hereafter made, advanced or executed; and that this section shall come into force on September 1, 1934.
The Interest Act as it now stands places no limitation whatsoever on the rate of interest which may be charged. That is left to agreement between the lender and the borrower. The Bank Act, however, does fix a limit of seven per cent which may be charged by any bank on a loan. Amendments to the act recently passed make this seven per cent clause effective, ail though it was not before. The bill I have introduced asks for a limitation on the rate of interest which may be charged on real estate mortgages. According to evidence given before the banking and commerce committee last year real estate mortgages on farms are estimated at $726,000,000 and urban mortgages are estimated at $765,000,000, making a total of $1,491,000,000.
I should like to deal first with farm mortgages. Last year the committee received a statement from the bureau of statistics to the effect that the rate of interest charged on all mortgages in Canada, rural and urban, would average 6.90 per cent. I think it is fair to estimate that the average rate on farm mortgages would be at least seven per cent. This would make the interest charge to be met by the farmers of Canada on their mortgages approximate the sum of $50,000,000. I think everyone will agree that this interest, if it is to be paid, must come from the production on these farms. Everyone knows that the farmers have been going through very difficult times for the last four years. From 1928 to 1932 the net revenue of the farms of Canada fell by 57 per cent; in other words the revenue in 1932 was only 43 per cent of the revenue in 1928. The costs of the farmer and the expenditures necessary to production were not reduced to anything like the same extent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In some cases more.

So really the farmer has been producing in most cases at a loss, and has had no margin whatever out of which to pay interest, though for the last four years the interest charges have been continuing. In 1932 the net agricultural revenue in Canada is estimated by the bureau of statistics at S600 per farm, out of which the farmer had to pay interest, taxes and other cash payments, and on the average there were six persons who had to get their living from each farm. The interest burden is becoming intolerable, and

here is a very good example of what is going on. I have here an article from the Renfrew Mercury, repeated in the Ottawa Citizen:
Not many weeks ago, not a hundred miles from Renfrew, an Ontario trust company sold a fine, well-cultivated farm which had come back on their hands, for less than $2 (two dollars) per acre. Why? There had been loaned' upon the farm, on the security of a mortgage, an amount of several thousand dollars, but the mortgagor, the farmer who had owned the farm, could not meet the payments; the price of farm products was not sufficient to pay for wages, living expenses, mortgage interest and taxes. So the farm was sold for less than it would have brought nearly one hundred years ago.
Something has happened to the farmer's dollar-it has shrunk in value, failed to keep pace with the fluctuations in prices of the things which the farmer has to pay for, for the farmer's currency is the products he grows or raises or manufactures ...
It is too much to expect that the problems of Canadian agriculture are capable of being solved over-night-especially with Canada's present defective monetary system-but this much is certain, that the present fiscal policy of the Dominion is inimical to the best interests of agriculture and until the policy of exploiting the farmer for the benefit of the non-producer, of crushing down agriculture with a burden of invisible indirect taxation, and of taking away with the one hand any benefit extended to agriculture with the other, is abandoned, the "fair exchange value" will never be experienced by the Canadian farmer, and the return of prosperity to the nation will be deferred.
The burden of interest is felt very keenly by the farmer because, as I said before, it can only come out of the margin the farmer has over his costs of production. To-day, as for the past year or two, farmers are being urged to sign mortgages bearing rates of interest of seven per cent and eight per cent. I have personal knowledge of farmers who have paid eight per cent for twenty years and still owe the principal. Had they been charged only five per cent the other three per cent would have amortized the loan and the debt would have been retired by this time. I admit that some relief legislation has been introduced, but it is not in any way sufficient to deal with the existing situation.
Let me direct the attention of the house to legislation passed in Brazil on December 1, 1933. I am quoting from the monthly bulletin of the British chamber of commerce of Brazil, and this quotation is taken from one of the official journals:
Whereas:-
Agricultural production contributed almost the whole of the sacrifice demanded of the country for the purpose of national exchange defence measures;

owing to the crisis having become general, and all the products thereof have suffered a considerable reduction in value;
such reduction in value has placed almost all agriculturists-or, it may be said, national economy itself, since its foundations rest on agriculture-in a position of serious difficulty;
in such cases it is incumbent upon the public authority to act in the matter, taking the necessary steps for the defence of national interests intermingled with those of private individuals;
The head of the provisional government of the republic of the United States of Brazil, by virtue of the powers conferred on him by article 1 of decree No. 19,398 of November 11, 1930, decrees that:
Art. 1. As from the date of this decree, the amount of all debts of agriculturists contracted before 30th June, 1933, against real or pledged security, is hereby reduced by fifty per cent.
I should like to direct the attention of the house to that paragraph once more;
-the amount of all debts of agriculturists contracted before 30th June. 1933. against real or pledged security, is hereby reduced by fifty per cent.
In the next paragraph debts contracted after June 30, 1933, provided they constitute renewals of old debts, are also included under the provisions of the decree.
My time is almost up, but before sitting down I would say in regard to urban mortgages that the ability of the people to pay is fixed by the income they receive. To indicate the extent to which their ability to pay has been reduced may I point out that in 1929 the wages paid by the Canadian National railways amounted to S177,000,000 while in 1932 they dropped to $106,000,000, and that is a good indication of what has happened to the wages of our people generally.
Those two great classes of people, the farmers and the labouring people, are responsible for most of the interest which must be paid on real estate mortgages. Their ability to pay has in many cases almost completely disappeared, and I would urge the house to give consideration to this measure which asks that a limitation of five per cent be placed on real estate mortgages entered into after this time.
