Of all asinine sections to
put in the bill, this is certainly one. I have some Doukhobors in my constituency and if one of these should happen to be the son of

Dominion Franchise Act
a Doukhobor living in British Columbia, he would be disqualified notwithstanding the fact that he was a good citizen. These Doukho-bors are as good citizens as any others in this country. On their behalf I resent this section.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
I quite realize why this section was inserted; it was because of the troubles that have occurred in British Columbia through the refusal of certain citizens to observe the laws of the country. However, I want to go on record as being absolutely opposed to any sect or any religious community being singled out by name, as they are in this legislation, and disfranchised by the parliament of Canada. I am entirely opposed to the lawless practices of some members of this sect; I am absolutely in favour of law and order being observed, but it will be noted that in the statutes of British Columbia they are not mentioned by name. The minister will find that the provincial act of 1931 states:
-that every person exempted or entitled to claim exemption, or who on production of any certificate might have become or would now be entitled to claim exemption from military service by reason of certain orders in council, and' every descendant of any such person, whether born in the province or elsewhere, shall be disqualified from voting.
I may be incorrectly informed, but my information is that certain Doukhobors in British Columbia served overseas with the Canadian forces. It will be noted that the next section in the British Columbia act includes Japanese who saw service overseas with the Canadian forces, and the same thing is done in the federal act. It seems to be exceedingly unfair to disfranchise the sons of Doukhobors or naturalized Doukhobors or even Doukhobors who served overseas. I think we are adopting the wrong principle when we are bound more or less by the terms of a provincial statute. I am opposed to any sect being disfranchised by name. If it is necessary to do so, I would rather see it done some other way. We grant certain privileges to other people who served overseas, so why should we not give it to these if there be any? The sons or grandsons of these people who are born in British Columbia may migrate to Yorkton or some other constituency, and they will be disfranchised. If these people refuse to obey our laws they should be punished, but I think disfranchisement is the wrong form of punishment. It is an invidious distinction. I hold no brief for these people as I think they deserved the punishment which the attorney general and the government of the day in British Columbia meted
out to them, but I think it is a bad precedent for this parliament to follow. I sympathize with the troubles of the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling), but this is the wrong principle to follow.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: I spoke in connection with this matter the other day. It is a bad principle to have a federal law dependent upon provincial laws. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) will recognize at once that that is not a good way to pass federal legislation. In connection with this particular sect, probably only one out of twenty Doukhobors are members of the Sons of Freedom, who have been causing some trouble to the government. The rest of the Doukhobors are good citizens, as is shown by the report of the royal commission appointed some years ago by the British Columbia government This fact is known to those who are resident in Saskatchewan. This legislation is something new in the history of the country. It is directed not against a national group but against a religious group. It is a very serious thing. Apart from the fanatical outburst of a few of their number, the only thing against the group as a whole is the fact that they refuse to bear arms. The whole country was shocked a few months ago when certain individuals were refused citizenship in the United States because they refused to bear arms.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: They also refuse to wear clothes.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
I am referring to certain individuals in the United States who were refused citizenship, one of them being a woman, another a Canadian of high standing. We all thought at that time that it was a serious thing when individuals were penalized and refused citizenship for no other reason than their conscientious objection to participation in military service.
I am sure that this section will involve all kinds of complications. There is a large number of Doukhobors resident in Saskatchewan; there is a smaller number in Alberta and quite a large group in British Columbia. There is an invidious distinction between those in Saskatchewan and Alberta and those in British Columbia. As the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) has pointed out, all sorts of complications will arise by these people passing from one province to the other. Only a few weeks ago I met an old friend of mine who is now a lawyer in Saskatoon. I have known him since his undergraduate days, almost twenty years ago. He is a Doukhobor who in his earlier days was given an education by the Quakers in
Dominion Franchise Act

Pennsylvania. I am sorry to bring personal matters into this discussion but the matter is such a serious one that I think I am justified in doing so. The wife of my Doukhobor friend is the daughter of a former lecturer at Queen's university. If this prominent lawyer, who was a candidate in the recent Saskatchewan provincial elections, should migrate to British Columbia he would be disqualified, and his descendants, the children of the daughter of a former lecturer of Queen's, would also be disqualified.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Where was he born?

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
He is I think Canadian born, and the only objection which could be taken to him would be on account of his parentage. This man has received a splendid education in the eastern states which he completed in Saskatchewan university where he was one of the popular students. He then took a course in law and has been practising in Saskatoon for a number of years. It is absurd that a man of that character and his children should be disfranchised. It is a wholly new doctrine. Not only is the individual discriminated against because of his religious beliefs but such discrimination extends to his descendants. Most of us have assumed that a man's religion is a matter of his own choice, and that if he wishes to do so he may repudiate the religion of his parents. But that is impossible under this law. The section enumerates certain classes who may not vote. Subsection (xii) reads:
Every Doukhobor person in the province of British Columbia, and every descendant of any such person whether born in that province or elsewhere, who is by the law of that province disqualified from voting at an election of a member of the legislative assembly of that province.
It seems to me a most indefensible piece of legislation and one that is bound to cause very serious trouble. I think the minister would be well advised to withdraw it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
To begin with I do not think the minister has carried out the intention of the government in the way the section is worded. I recall that the Prime Minister, when discussing the franchise bill before, said that any disqualification respecting Doukhobors would apply only to Doukhobors voting in British Columbia. As this is worded, it would if he happened to be a descendant of British Columbia Doukhobors disqualify a Doukhobor in Saskatchewan or Alberta or any other province. The error is due to the transposition of a clause. In order to carry out the intention of the government it should read: "Every Doukhobor person in the prov-

ince of British Columbia, and every descendant in the province of British Columbia
of any such person..." That would correct
the first error; as it is at present worded the provision is contrary to the government's intention as proposed. A further reading of the section would disclose that it carries with it the right of a Doukhobor born in British Columbia to vote in another province if he happens to go to another province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: No doubt about that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
I am pointing
this out in regard to the drafting. Apart from that, on the principle involved I agree with other hon. gentlemen; I do not think that persons of any class or race should be disqualified on the score of their religious belief, and especially that one should not go back to the Old Testament times and seek to visit what we regard as the iniquities of fathers upon their descendants to the third and fourth generation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
The words suggested by
my right hon. friend should be inserted. After the word "person", in line 31, there should be added the words "in the province of British Columbia".

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
Would
it not be better, and would it not obtain the same result if you struck out the word "Doukhobor" altogether and also the words "and every descendant of every such person" so that it would read: "Every person in the province of British Columbia who is by the law of that province disqualified from voting", and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
That would disqualify a
lot of other people besides Doukhobors. This is the law of British Columbia and we have adopted that law, and while it is true that in the British Columbia legislation the word "Doukhobor" is not used, I think we are more candid about it and have put it in. The idea of the section is that they shall not vote if they are not entitled to vote in British Columbia-not in any other province but only in British Columbia. To make that clear I move that the words "in the province of British Columbia" be inserted after the word "person" in line 31, as suggested by my right hon. friend.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
I will not be satisfied with any mere amendment to this section. I want to know whether we are going back to the days of the thumbscrew and the inquisition in matters of religion. Now that is not a dream. There are many of us who -have

Dominion Franchise Act
not much religion, and you find others with too much. It seems to me we require in Canada some with too much in order to preserve a half decent average. Here we are, supposedly a Christian community, making the franchise depend upon the religion of certain people. The Doukhobors are a distinctly religious sect, fanatical if you like. They take the ground, some of them, and at times, that they can worship the Creator better in a naked condition than clothed or partially clothed. Well, we sometimes run across other people with peculiarities in religious matters, but if they are genuine, is that a good ground for disfranchising them? How will that cure them? I will not say anything of a threatening nature, but I would not want anything better than this in an election to campaign with against the government. The government can leave it there if they like. There are other heinous provisoes connected with the franchise which appeared in the bill when it was first drafted, and when the proper time comes we shall not forget any of these attempts to disfranchise good citizens. As regards these Doukhobors, I say it would be a standing disgrace to Canada, as it would be to any Christian country, to pass this section. It is a fine example of reactionary Toryism when applied to the franchise with respect to certain people who have cast their lot in with us in Canada. I know something about the Doukhobors. We run across them as farm labourers on adjoining farms, and I know that they are as a whole a hard working, conscientious people, industrious, thrifty and, if you like, God-fearing. The hon. member for Yorkton has not exaggerated their many good qualities., I do not know how they vote and I do not care. A lot of them did not vote at all in the early days as a matter of principle, but that is not the point. Just imagine what is being done now in this day, when we seem to be developing a more active spiritual religion, a real live religion, stimulated by the Oxford group and other movements of that kind. While that is going on, within the shadow and even within this building, we have this government penalizing a religious sect and saying to them, "You cannot vote and be citizens of Canada so long as you hold such and such religious beliefs." It is no wonder the Minister of Justice is getting as red as a bubbly-jock. It shows there is some hope for him yet. He is getting white behind the gills and red in the wattles; that shows also there is some conscience left in him. I appeal to him now not to disgrace us all by committing this unseemly act. If it were only disgracing an already disgraced government it
would not be so bad, but it will disgrace this whole parliament, the Senate as well, because they will be expected to swallow it. I wonder, is that the artist sitting in front of the minister, the artist who drafted this blooming act as well as the War-time Elections Act. If he is so artistic as to draft this bill he should be able to draft another one equally good and avert this political crime.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Be fair; the man cannot defend himself.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Oh well, I will take on anyone either in parliament or out of it as far as that goes.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: When he can't talk.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: The minister ought to be ashamed to have the draftsman of this act and of the War-time Elections Act sitting in the house before him, and trying to make out it was just a memorandum they gave the conference members on this side, when it was a full fledged act like any other.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Deliberately drafted.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Yes, and deliberately deceiving us into thinking it was only a memorandum. It was bad enough to draft the thing, but to come here and brazenly falsify it is a thousand times worse. The Doukhobors don't do anything like this anyhow; they are usually truthful. What they are they are, and they are not ashamed of it. But this government, hiding behind the draftsman, brings down this kind of legislation, this kind of heathen stuff, to push through parliament.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite need have no concern about any injustice to the Doukhobors. Had they had just a little experience with them, they would not be disposed to extend very much sympathy. For the past fourteen years prior to the last election there has never been a Doukhobor vote cast in British Columbia, although within the past fourteen years many Doukhobors bom in Canada have been entitled to exercise the franchise. It was only at the last election that they ever were encouraged or signified any intention to vote. I assure hon. gentlemen opposite that could they have witnessed the scenes in West Kootenay at the last federal election they would all have been quite willing to have disfranchised this religious sect. There can be no sense of responsibility and no individualism in a member of any group in which the leader dictates and dominates the marking of the ballot. Just prior to the last election the Doukhobors in
Dominion Franchise Act

British Columbia were called together by their leader, Peter Verigin; there they were instructed just how to mark their ballots and they marked them with all the precision and accuracy that any well trained and intelligent Canadian could use; indeed, more accurately, as was indicated by the fact that out of 248 ballots cast at one poll not a single ballot was spoiled and every one was marked accurately with a cross after the Liberal candidate's name.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Is that why they are being disfranchised, because they voted Liberal?

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
No. To those who may be disposed to think that this may be a political advantage, we will admit it is a political advantage and a very pronounced one, but it is a political advantage to every candidate regardless of what party he may be affiliated with. There is no individualism in permitting a leader or one man practically to vote for any one group. There are 4,500 Doukhobors in West Kootenay and there are 1,000 more in the adjoining federal district of Yale. Of the 4,500 in West Kootenay, about 2.000 have the franchise and they could very well have exercised it at the last election had there not been an endeavour to prevent them. In other words some registrars did not make a return of their lists to the returning officers. Those lists came to light just at the last day.
Let me say just this to satisfy my hon. friends opposite: the Doukhobors came here in 1898 under an order in council passed in 1896. They were given large tracts of land; they were otherwise bonused or provided with implements and with some money and they went upon the land. We heard very little of them for a while until they moved to West Kootenay some twenty odd years ago. They have absolutely no regard for Canadian law. They will not admit of any provincial law. They will not register births, deaths or marriages. There is not anybody who can challenge a Doukhobor and tell who he is and what is his age. More than that, they have just exercised their own inclinations by the burning of schools; they did not want their children to go to school and their action in that regard in the last few years has resulted in the burning of some thirty-five schools in British Columbia. The situation became so tense in the federal district of Yale that the people there had to guard the schools with floodlights. Then the Doukhobors had their nude parades which cost British
	*
Columbia some 850,000 for keeping Jhose Doukhobors at Okalla and they have cost the federal government many thousands of dollars for the creation of this penitentiary at the coast.
One specific agreement under the order in council states that the Doukhobors should be exempt from military service and that is their greatest and keenest desire. Let me assure hon. gentlemen opposite, regardless of what they say, the Doukhobors do not want the vote. Just about two weeks ago they had a mass meeting and strange as this may seem to hon. gentlemen opposite, that body of Doukhobors passed resolutions at their mass meeting presided over by their leader, Peter Verigin, extending the most grateful acknowledgment to this government for having indicated that it would disfranchise them at the federal election. They simply took the ground that this disqualification confirmed the agreement under the order in council made in 1896 which exempted them from military service, and that is precisely what they wanted.
Further, after that mass meeting the younger element of Doukhobors, a society known as the Doukhobors Youths, gathered at a public meeting within the past ten days and recorded resolutions again thanking this federal government for having disqualified them, and this was done simply on the ground that the government's action confirmed the terms of the order in council exempting them from military service.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
May I ask my hon. friend this question:	This government has not
disqualified them yet. Were they not a little too soon with their resolutions?

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: I know that, but the press reports to that effect were out nearly a month ago.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: They relied upon press reports. I would ask my hon. friend this further question: How is disfranchisement going to help the situation? Will they wear clothes if they are disfranchised?

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: I hope they will when the hon. member for Cartier comes to British Columbia.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
The tale told by the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) has not that sickly sentimental flavour that some of the speeches we have heard to-night have had, but it happens to be true. This is not a question of religion; it is one of behaviour, which is quite a different matter. An attempt has been made to show that these Doukhobors

Dominion Franchise Act
are a downtrodden, God-fearing people. It is not part of their rdigion to go without clothes; that is not why they take their clothes off. They do this to show their displeasure when they are asked to obey the laws of the land; they stage these nude parades in order to show their displeasure.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: They want to tell the naked truth.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
It is easy to trot out one particular case. My hon. friend beside me (Mr. Woodsworth) talks of an isolated case of a professor, but they are not all professors. The hon. member for West Kootenay talked about their burning schools and I think he mentioned thirty-five schools, but he did not tell of the Doukhobors bombing a school when a poor young white woman teacher was in it. The teachers had to be taken from the schools because their nerves gave way. The hon. member did not tell the committee of the time that a train was bombed and their leader and a member of the legislature were killed. He did not tell of the Canadian Pacific having to spend enormous sums in guarding railway bridges because the Doukhobors had a playful habit of blowing them up too. That does not sound so God-fearing if you put the matter in that light.
There is one point I should like to speak about, and that- is the remark of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) when he said that it was outrageous or unbelievable or something like that, that the federal franchise should be dominated by or from the provincial legislature. That is exactly what we are bound to do, to follow the provincial law in that regard. The question was brought up some years ago in connection with the admission of Hindus. My hon. friend to my right was very enthusiastic on behalf of them, I remember. I heard the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen, then leader of the opposition, most emphatically lay down that principle, and I rather think the right hon,. leader of the opposition to-day spoke along the same lines, but he is here to contradict me if I am wrong. At any rate I know that Mr. Meighen laid it down as an accepted axiom of constitutional law under the British North America Act that we in this parliament were bound to follow the inhibitions or any other restrictions made by the provinces.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: I may be strong on the constitution but I never said that.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: I naturally associate the word "constitution" with the right hon. leader of the opposition. I do not think he will say that he did not support the idea that we ought to follow the provincial legislatures in their franchise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: No, I do not think I ever agreed to anything of the kind.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Then I will take it back; he ought to know what he said. But I remember distinctly-Mr. Meighen is not here to contradict me-I know I quoted him in contradiction to my hon. friend here, who would not let a chance like that slip.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: My recollection is the same as that of my leader.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: You see the extreme partisanship. He only thinks the same as his leader. Mr. Meighen said it-and even if I am deprived of Mr. Meighen's backing I can point to history: we have always done that, always followed any inhibition that the provinces created in regard to the franchise.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if that is true in regard to the disfranchisement of women in the province of Quebec? They have a vote in the federal not in the provincial elections.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: And we are in favour of their having a vote here.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: The question came up the last time this Franchise Act was put through, in 1924 I think; the same question was raised in connection with the Japanese voting in British Columbia, and it was decided under the leadership of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, at any rate he did carry into our franchise the inhibition against orientals that existed in British Columbia. That is what I am saying to-day, that the province has the right to say what their own franchise shall be. The matter was taken to the privy council on one occasion in connection with a Japanese called Yatagama or some such name.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Has the amendment that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) moved been carried?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: The insertion of the words "in the province of British Columbia" in line 31 after the word "person" is the amendment.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
If I am in order I would move that paragraph (xii) be struck out of the bill.
Dominion Franchise Act

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
I should very much like to second that motion. I am going to take the opportunity of making some further comments in regard to this little-understood sect- I have personally known them since they were brought here under the late Sir Clifford Sifton who was then Minister of the Interior. They were granted at that time certain privileges, among others that of living in communities and of exemption from military service. When Sir Clifford Sifton was superseded by Hon. Frank Oliver there was a change of policy on the part of the department; they insisted that the Doukhobors should take up individual homesteads and swear allegiance, which was contrary to their rather peculiar ideas. So they gave up lands which some have valued at $10,000,000, a great many of them subsequently going on small farms for themselves, breaking with the parent community. A number of the members of the community proper then migrated to British Columbia, and established a community at the junction of the Kootenay and Columbia rivers. Undoubtedly, as I remember the late president of the university of British Columbia saying to me, they have managed to accomplish through their cooperative efforts in that rather rough country what the ordinary individual settler had been unable to do. Anyone who visits their community there and inspected their jam factories and logging operations and so on cannot but recognize that at least from a material standpoint they have made good. Certain of the merchants in the town of Nelson several years ago set up an agitation against them because they were buying by wholesale rather than from the retail stores. A commission was appointed by the British Columbia government to investigate the whole situation. Had I known this matter would come up I would have had the volume here to quote from the report of the commission, but I remember it very distinctly. The report of that commission stated that there was no crime whatever among them, that they were good citizens in every respect, but according to their religious ideas they would not participate in the ordinary affairs of government. That was a number of years ago.
From the first there have been in that community, I quite frankly admit, a certain number of people who have been fanatical. Personally I am inclined to think that some ' of them are a little crazy-

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: They are not alone.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
-and they have fantastic ideas. It was this particular group that caused trouble when they went to Win-

nipeg some years ago, having abandoned their homes and implements and so on. They had to be returned. Every once in a while this fanaticism breaks out. There are to-day three distinct groups. I should say that while about eight or nine thousand Doukhobors came to the country forty years ago there must be *nearly twenty thousand in Canada to-day. There are three groups; first the community Doukhobors proper under the jurisdiction of Peter Verigin; second the non-community Doukhobors who have broken with the colony and who have individual farms and homesteads. Most of those in Saskatchewan now are non-community Doukhobors, descendants of the original immigrants who have gone off on their own and are in every respect Canadian citizens. Then, third, there is this little fanatical group called the Sons of Freedom. That is the group that has caused the greater part of the trouble in British Columbia and also whenever there have been outbreaks in Saskatchewan. They refused to obey even Peter Verigin-and perhaps I may say that although the first Peter Verigin was an able man I believe the present man is not a very desirable type of citizen. Nevertheless he was regarded as the religious head, and his followers gave him their allegiance.
Reference has been made to some acts of terrorists. Someone bombed a train; Peter Verigin was on that train and was killed. It has never been established who bombed the train. The Doukhobors themselves are inclined to blame the Sons of Freedom. I talked to the engine driver on the train concerned, and he told me he believed it was a prospector, who had some dynamite aboard and who was also killed at the time. He did not think the Doukhobors were guilty of the outrage. I do not know.
Then we find that in British Columbia a number of schools were burned. The people who follow Peter Verigin, the community Doukhobors, believe it was done by these Sons of Freedom, and they were so much afraid of the Sons of Freedom that they called in the mounted police and the government officials to protect them against this small fanatical sect. I could show that by reference to the Nelson News, in which a good many documents were published a few years ago. So that although a certain number of Doukhobors were presumably guilty of outrages, it was never proved in any court but it was believed by the Doukhobors themselves that it was the Sons of Freedom who were guilty, and certainly it is the so-called Sons of Freedom who have given the government such trouble. But my point to-night is that

Dominion Franchise Act
it is not fair, when perhaps not more than one out of twenty belongs to the Sons of Freedom, to penalize the other nineteen-twentieths of the Doukhobors in this country.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: And their descendants.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
And their descendants. The statement is made that they do not want their children to go to school. That was true a great many years ago. That is still true of the Sons of Freedom; it is not true of the great majority of the Douk-hobor people. For years I have been closely in touch with those people in Saskatchewan. Some years ago I had occasion, while working under a government bureau, to make a rather careful analysis of the situation existing among the non-English speaking peoples, and I found the great part of the Doukhobors in Saskatchewan attending school in the districts in which they lived. There is no trouble there. Two years ago I took occasion to revisit the community near Nelson, British Columbia. I visited four or five schools and talked with the teachers. One of the teachers was a young Doukhobor woman; the other three were Canadian born girls. I asked one of the teachers who had been there for six or eight or ten years, "Do you see anything of these parades?" She said, "In all the years I have been here I have never seen a nude Doukhobor." I asked, "What about the education of the children?" She said, '(Practically all the children in this district are now attending public school, and a finer class of children you would not see anywhere." I saw them in their classes; I saw them out on the playing fields, and they were a fine type of children. They came from the neighbouring districts to attend these schools.
I think it is absurd that the newspapers, with the idea of getting some picturesque stories, should have played up these nude parades to such an extent that it has given the 'Canadian public the idea that the great majority of the people are fanatics. That is not true. I quite admit that it is true of a certain sect, but that is just my point. Penalize the people who refuse to obey our laws, if you like; that is right, but do not penalize merely because of religious ideas. It very well may be that the present Peter Verigin may want to keep his people from exercising the franchise. I can quite understand that. As someone has said, he is a little dictator, but why should we heed the behests of Peter Verigin? I submit that among the younger people especially there is a decided move to participate in the life of the Canadian people
which should be encouraged. If we do encourage that move it will be only a few years until these troubles will have passed away with the older generation. If, however, we keep them isolated and refuse to grant them citizenship with the rest of us undoubtedly there will be trouble all along the line.
It has been stated that one individual taught them how to vote; apparently the shoe is pinching because he taught them to vote Liberal instead of Conservative. I think it is absurd that these people should be disfranchised merely because they are told by one of their spiritual leaders how to vote. If the newspapers are right, in the last Ontario election some of the clergy told the people of Ontario that they should vote Liberal.

It is not the course of wisdom to play into the hands, if I may use that expression, of the one dictator we have there, Peter Verigin. I hope the amendment moved by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) will be accepted. The only possible justification for legislation of this kind would be if it were confined very strictly to the people who have broken the criminal laws of this country. I do want to plead very strongly for this section of our community, and I wish to protest against certain religious tenets being made the basis for disfranchisement.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINTMENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has given the committee the benefit of a most specious piece of special pleading. He has stated that he has been well acquainted with these people ever since they reached Canada. I very much regret that, according to my experience with them, his acquaintanceship with the Doukhobors has not benefited them. The hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Ealing) has recounted some of the behaviour of the Doukhobors in his constituency at the time of the 1930 election; may I, in a very few moments, carry the chapter one page further.
Five days before the general election of 1930 Peter Verigin arrived in the town of Grand Forks. The Doukhobors had not been placed on the voters' lists; they had not asked to be placed on the lists, neither had the enumer-

Dominion Franchise Act

ators asked them if they desired to be on the lists. Peter Verigin instructed them to swear themselves on the lists on the day of the poll, and they flocked to the polling places for that purpose. They came in such numbers that by the time the poll was closed by no means all had succeeded in swearing themselves on the lists, for to a large extent the men resembled each other like two peas, and 'the women were so much alike that it was necessary to challenge each one in the attempt at least to record the name of the individual. They voted. I have not the clear evidence of how they voted that the hon. member for West Kootenay has in regard to one certain poll, but I have this very fair inference, that in the polling divisions concerned my majority was reduced to a certain extent at each poll. Therefore it follows, to my satisfaction at least, that the Doukhobors voted Liberal en bloc. That has nothing whatever to do with the case before us, except that if they voted en bloc in one direction, there is no reason why they should not vote en bloc in another direction at another time, and personally I do not consider that the franchise in Canada should be so exercised.
There is one other incident to which I should like to direct the attention of the committee; I refer to the happenings on the hills above Grand Forks, where the Doukhobors live, at the time an attempt was made to take the census. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre describes these people as virtuous, as having children who make good scholars and as a happy, contented, industrious people. When the census officer went to their community he endeavoured to obtain the information that was required. They are a people, as the committee already has been informed, who have always snapped their fingers at provincial statutes such as the vital statistics act. There is no record of when they were born or where they were born. They refused to give the information; three attempts were made on three successive days to secure the information required for the census. At last a solicitor employed by the census bureau accompanied the enumerators to endeavour to explain to these people that no harm would come from filling out these forms so that the statistics of Canada might be complete. I am sorry to say that an attempt was made to take the clothes off the solicitor. I must draw the attention of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to the fact that the leaders of those unruly proceedings were two girls who had been through high school.

Let me recount one further incident. In the summer of 1931 or perhaps of 1932, the citizens of Grand Forks, utterly weary of the difficulties they had experienced in watching their schools, in flood-lighting them, in endeavouring to protect their water intake in the river and so on, called a meeting of their prominent citizens, to which the provincial member and myself were asked to come. It was a meeting of the city council, the board of trade, representatives of the church and representatives of the various social organizations of that little town, and we heard what they had to say with regard to the Doukhobors. I should like certain hon. members who are advancing contrary views to have been present on that occasion and to have seen a side of the picture exactly opposite to that described by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and several other hon. members. The farmers on the outskirts of Grand1 Forks whose farms lie on the borders of the Doukhobor community not only suffer from fright but suffer from actual danger to life and limb. The Doukhobors behave with disgusting indecency in front of their farms. The children and the growing up young men and women cannot comport themselves in reasonable freedom because of the danger of molestation from the Doukhobors who certainly do not regard clothes as an absolute necessity.
I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) make the statement-if I understood him correctly-that some of the Doukhobors in that area had seen military service.

I should like to check up on the remark that I made a moment ago. I now have Hansard before me, and after consulting it I must apologize to the right hon. leader of the opposition. The allusion was not to him, but to Sir Wilfrid Laurier. At page 4647 of Hansard for 1923 I spoke as follows:
It is a British Columbia problem for this reason: the franchise invariably originates in the province. It is entirely a provincial matter. I would quote Sir Wilfrid Laurier who in 1917 laid down in most emphatic language in paragraph after paragraph that the true basis of our dominion franchise under the British North America Act is the provincial franchise. He used the word "originates." The franchise originates in the province and then has to be translated into the dominion act. The right hon. leader of the opposition,-
That was Mr. Meighen.

I suggest the proper transposition would be to begin the clause with the words, "In the province of British Columbia" and thus obviate ambiguity. The clause would read:
In the province of British Columbia every Doukhobor person and every descendant of any such person, whether born in that province or elsewhere,-

The criticism some of imy remarks incited render it necessary for me to make some further observations. I happened to be a member of the first Saskatchewan government, and one of our first duties after taking office in 1905 was to deal with
74726-284J
some of these Doukhobor parades. I remember them distinctly. There was no resentment against authority at that time; the parades were part of their religious rites and performances. I do not know what later developments were; it may be that in later years it developed into an action of resentment, as the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) has said. I can say, however, thht in eaiilier years it was an act of worship towards God. We found in the administration of justice through the department of the attorney general that a great deal could be done by tempering justice with mercy, and fair dealing with kindness. The history of the world indicates that if you undertake to persecute a people for their religious beliefs, no matter how absurd you may think they are, you will just make them more determined, and bring the very worst out of them. As a matter of fact, was not the Christian church disseminated all over the world by persecution? I ask you that. The blood of the martyrs was said to be the seed of the church. The point is that in this instance we may not confine such action to the Doukhobors, because if we set our hand towards establishing this kind of precedent, we do not know who or what people will bring down the wrath of the Tory government next.
I do not know how many hon. members can recall the advent of the Salvation Army into Canada. In those days I was attending school in the old town of Perth. The Army did things which appeared strange to us, and were garbed much the same as to-day They beat their tom-toms just the same, and they sang just the same. They assembled in front of the hotel doors just the same and offered up prayers for the guests, and they had pitchers of water thrown on them from upper windows as a kind of reception or collection. That was the only collection they got in those days of nearly sixty years ago. When we look back to those days we have no cause to be proud of ourselves. To-day the Salvation Army is one of the most respected religious bodies in the world. But, because they were different from the rest of us, we seemed to think that hating them would count as righteousness into us. Civilization based on hating some one or some thing is not on a good foundation; yet that was our attitude towards the Salvation Army. I was born a severe hater of everything that was French and everything that was Catholic. Anything I can do to rectify that mistake, that terrible mistake of my early training, I shall do for the rest of my life. I was wrong; absolutely wrong. And towards men and women who worship at the same

shrine as we do, and who worship the same Godhead as we do, how dare we take this attitude, of persecution? That is all I have to say. I am in favour of the amendment to throw this section out of the bill higher than a kite.

I feel I should make
some observations, because if there were a vote I should feel I must vote in a certain way. I believe cooperation with a government is an elementary principle of civilization. Where would our institutions be if that were not the case? I am a great believer in freedom and in the rights of the individual, but I wonder where the country would be if all the different racial groups refused to cooperate. I think this question transcends the liberty of the individual. If the French, the English, the Irish, the Scotch, the Welsh, the Ukrainians and others all failed to cooperate in enforcing the laws of this country, where would we be? The first obligation of any individual is to cooperate with the state. I think that is elementary in the building up of our democratic institutions.

We may be forty years too late in discussing this problem. I should say that the proper way to deal with this matter is not to impose political persecution in a statute but to get these people out of the country if they refuse to obey our laws. We cannot afford to allow the great seal of Canada to be placed on a statute of persecution.

speechtext:
I understand that
closed lists are all settled now; I can feel the rope tightening around my neck already. And my hon. friends opposite will pull on the rope too. I know exactly what we are confronting, and what it is for. Apparently the house will have to go through one closed list experience in rural areas before they know what it means. I want to warn all on this side that they will have to be prepared to have about three thousands votes more than is necessary to elect them in some ridings in order to have enough to save them from defeat. I know what was done via the closed list route in 1896. It was not always in the law but in the way it was interpreted. The lasts were closed two days before the election, but they were not closed to the enumerators. During those two days it was not quite clear what the duties of the enumerator were, but an interpretation came from Ottawa to the Northwest Territories indicating that during that two days the enumerator could still put on the list what names he liked, and then the counterpart of that, he could still take off what names he liked. Good eligible names were taken off wholesale and others put on. It was easy to keep the ineligible from voting by means of active scrutineers, because such would have to be sworn, but those kept off were off. Let me say further, for the benefit of the government, that when you go too far in a matter of this kind it is so badly overdone that the people rebel. Dozens of enumerators refused to act after they learned the nature of the law, showing that in the Tory party there is a lot of fine white men in spite of the official Tories. They refused to act as deputy returning officers when they learned the .power of the enumerator and what they were expected to do. They turned in their resignations. A lot of others would not take advantage of the law as interpreted,
. while some of the others pretty nearly got tarred and feathered when they did take advantage of it. At a number of polls, as soon as we found on election day what was happening and saw what a large number were being disfranchised, we had to send out to the adjoining polls on fast horses all the runners we could get, with advice as to what the gov-vernment officials were doing to old and eligible voters. The result was that polls that never gave a majority in their lives gave one in 1896 because of the heinous crimes of the government and their officials of that day.
Dominion Franchise Act

So I am comparatively calm about the matter. There is a sense of justice among the electorate of Canada and I predict that in many districts this government will not be able to find the necessary officials to do the kind of dirty work that they expect them to do.

Dominion Elections Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When I give an inch you try to take everything.

We might as well recognize that the returning officer is to be appointed by this government; he will be a partisan officer, and is very likely to think that his duty is rather to the government than to the state. In cities, and after all that is where it is important, he will know by the cards returned that Mr. So and So, whose address is so and so, has moved from that place, or is dead, or has moved to another address, as the case may be. That returning officer inevitably will give that information to the Tory committee room.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps we had better
not insert this provision at all.

I would prefer it not to be there at all rather than give an undue advantage to one political party as compared with another. It is one way of checking the lists at government expense. If the same information is given both political parties well and good, but if it is not I think it is an outrage. I believe it is altogether uncalled for to give that advantage of using the mails and the money belonging to the people of Canada to one candidate rather than another. Though I like the suggestion and am quite willing to support my right hon. leader, if it does not work out fairly, equitably and reasonably for all parties then I would prefer that the suggestion be withdrawn.
I think the hon. gentleman is unduly suspicious of the men who will take the oath of office, but it would be very easy to have the postmaster not return these cards until after election day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Surely it would be very easy and simple to provide that the returning officer should make available to the candidate or his agent any information he may have as to notices returned for one reason or another. Instead of requiring the returning officer to notify both sides, if that
is expecting too much, simply require that the candidate or his agent shall have the right to obtain from the returning officer any information he may have with regard to cards that have been returned. The same information would then be available to both sides. It would not involve any expense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not wedded to it
at all.

This is a
good thing; it will be helpful to both the electors and the candidate. I believe the principle is sound. In Montreal during municipal elections every man who has his card goes to the polls. There is no canvassing; we are not obliged to go from door to door, and it saves an enormous amount of money to the candidate. If cards are returned they come back to the returning officer. There will not be so many of them if the list has been made properly. If I am the candidate in St. Henri I may find about five hundred cards returned. I try to find where those people have moved; then I give the new addresses to the returning officer, and he has a chance to send the cards out again. In Montreal if you mail a letter by ten o'clock in the morning it may be delivered the same afternoon, due to our efficient service, and if the address is wrong the card will be returned once more. I believe this is a very helpful suggestion, which will save a great deal of money to the candidate. We heard the Secretary of State say that in 1930 he spent $25,000 to be elected in the constituency of St. Lawrenee-St. George, so I humbly submit that this is an appropriate remedy, and that it should be easy so to frame the law as to prevent any abuse.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
These amendments provide for absentee voters casting their votes under these closed lists. This point was raised in the committee by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) and there has been considerable discussion over it. We have tried to adopt some of the provisions of the British Columbia act. These will be new sections and their provisions are limited to fishermen, sailors, lumbermen and miners.. They will apply to men who are more than twenty-five miles away from home on the date of the election. Such a man will be entitled to go
Dominion Elections Act

to the nearest polling division and obtain what is known as an absentee ballot. He then takes an oath which is attached to the ballot that he is on the list in some polling division within the province. He will be entitled to cast his vote and at the close of the poll the returning officer will count the absentee ballots and send them (o the appropriate division where the man is on the voters' list. If it is found that he is on the voters' list in that poll, his vote will be counted. The machinery to put this into force is quite complicated but I think we have it fairly complete. Therefore, I move:

101	(1) The manner of polling an absentee voter's vote shall be as follows:
(a)	The absentee voter may, at any time while the poll is open on polling day, apply to the deputy returning officer of that polling station which is nearest to the place where the voter is temporarily engaged or employed for leave to poll there an absentee voter's vote.
(b)	The deputy returning officer shall thereupon require the absentee voter to sign and depose to an affidavit in Form No. . That Form shall be printed on the back of all absentee voter's ballot papers. That affidavit shall be made before that officer. The ballot paper shall be in Form No. or such other form as the chief electoral officer shall prescribe and direct.
(c)	The deputy returning officer shall prepare the ballot paper for the voter by writing with ink on the counterfoil thereof the name of the electoral district to which the ballot appertains and by writing in the ballot with ink the names, residences and occupations of the candidates who, as shown by the printed list of candidates supplied to that officer pursuant to section one hundred and four of this act, have been nominated for the electoral district from which the voter is absent and to which his vote appertains. Only one name, description and occupation of a candidate shall be written in any one space in the ballot paper.
(d)	The deputy returning officer shall, before delivering the ballot paper to the absentee voter, fold and seal it, in such manner that the voter's name and signature, as writen in the affidavit, are concealed.
(e)	The deputy returning officer shall then
deliver the ballot paper to the voter, who shall mark and fold it in the manner provided by section	of this act and return it to the
deputy returning officer, who shall, in the presence of the voter, and without removing the counterfoil, place it in the ballot box to be thereafter dealt with as in the next following section of this act provided.
(2)	If in any case the absentee voter's ballot paper as supplied to the deputy returning officer has not sufficient spaces to contain the names of all the candidates the deputy returning officer shall add, by pasting thereto enough blanks in Form No. 43 to contain all such names. If in any case such ballot paper has more spaces than are required to contain the names of all the candidates the excess spaces shall be left blank.

102	(1) After the close of the poll, on the counting of the ballots, the deputy returning officer shall separate from the ordinary ballots of his polling station all absentee voters' ballots and segregate the latter into parcels according

to the respective electoral districts to which they appertain. He shall unfold and examine that portion of them which shows the name of the electoral district and the names of the candidates and make a list showing the number of votes cast for each candidate in each electoral district. It shall not be necessary for him to enter in such list the names of electoral districts or of candidates in respect of which or of whom no votes have been polled.
(2) After the examination of such ballots and the compilation of such lists the absent voters' ballots shall be refolded by the deputy returning officer so as not to disclose how the voters or any of them have marked such ballots. The deputy returning officer shall then place the absentee voters' ballots which appertain to each electoral district, together with a copy of the above mentioned list in so far as it relates to each electoral district, in separate envelopes, which he shall securely close, marking on the outside the name of the proper electoral district along with the words "Absentee Voters' Ballots," and he shall without delay forward them prepaid, by registered mail, properly addressed, to the returning officers of the electoral districts to which, respectively, they appertain. The deputy returning officer shall place in the ballot box copies of all such lists so mailed and he shall supply copies thereof to any candidate or to the agent of any candidate present who applies for the same. Finally, the deputy returning officer shall send by telegraph, or by the most speedy means available, to the returning officer of each electoral district in respect of which absentee voters' ballots have been polled at his polling station, a statement of the number of votes polled for each candidate as shown by the list prepared pursuant to subsection one of this section.
103. On the making of the final count pursuant to section	of this act the returning
officer in every electoral district shall open each parcel containing absent voters' ballots received from each deputy returning officer at any time before the completion of the final count, and shall deal with each parcel separately and in the following manner: Without unfolding that portion of the absent voter's ballot paper containing the candidates' names and without disclosing how the ballot paper is marked by the voter, he shall open that portion of the absent voter's ballot paper containing the signature and the affidavit of the voter. After examining each affidavit and finding that it is signed by the deponent and by the deputy returning officer before whom it was sworn, and finding that the deponent is a voter whose name appears on the list of voters for the polling division named in the affidavit, and that no person has in fact voted as such voter at the poll held in the polling division, the returning officer shall detach that portion of the ballot paper containing the names of the candidates from the counterfoil, and shall put the ballot without being opened into a ballot box to be used for the purpose of counting absent voters' ballots, and shall note on the list of voters against the number of the voter the fact that he has voted as an absent voter. If the returning officer finds that the name of the deponent does not appear on the list of voters for the electoral district named in the affidavit, or that some person has in fact voted as such voter at the poll held in the electoral
district he shall not count and he shall retain the whole ballot paper unseparated as to any part thereof and unopened as to that portion of the ballot paper containing the candidates' name. After all absent voters' ballot papers have been dealt with, the returning officer shall proceed to count the votes given for each candidate and in his statement showing the result of the election he shall take into account all absentee voters' ballots found by him as aforesaid to be countable.
104 (1) Immediately after the close of nominations on nomination day the returning officer of every electoral district in Canada. shall transmit by telegraph to the chief electoral officer the names, addresses and occupations of all candidates whose nominations are in his hands, as these names addresses and occupations will appear on the ballot papers of such returning officer's electoral district. The chief electoral officer shall cause sufficient printed copies of the applicable names, addresses and occupations of candidates to be made to enable every returning officer in every electoral district of Canada to supply to every deputy returning officer in that returning officer's electoral district a list of the names, addresses and occupations of every candidate nominated in every electoral district in the province in which such returning officer's electoral district is situate and of the electoral districts wherein such candidate, respectively, have been nominated.
(2) The chief electoral officer shall, in time to enable performance by returning officers of the provisions of sections ninety-nine to one hundred and five, inclusive, of this act. transmit or cause to be transmitted to all returning officers sufficient copies of lists of names, addresses and occupations of candidates, absentee voters' ballot papers and Forms No. 42 and No. 43 to enable every returning officer to transmit to every deputy returning officer w-ith-in that returning officer's electoral district (which operation that returning officer shall execute) in time for use on polling day, sufficient copies of such documents for use at and for the purposes of each deputy returning officer's polling station, to enable compliance with sections ninety-nine to one hundred and five, inclusive, of this act.
105. Every provision of this act which can apply to absentee voters and absentee voting as provided for in sections ninety-nine to one hundred and four, inclusive, of this act, shall apply thereto.

Now that is a lengthy proposal and the form of the ballot paper in blank is attached. It has been represented to me that in many provinces, particularly in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia, there are frequently large bodies of men engaged in remote places-
And Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -and it is impossible to have them poll their vote without bringing them long distances. This will simply provide that the absentee may vote and his vote may be counted at his own polling division and he may transfer it or vote at the poll nearest to the place where he is working, and anywhere within his own province that vote may be counted if he is on the list. The machinery is pretty intricate, but on the whole I approve of the proposal and I think we should add it to the purposes in respeet of the four classes mentioned in the proposal.
Will the minister look at the definition of miner? It sounded to me as if there was no inclusive class similar to the definition of lumberman.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. member could make it more inclusive I should be glad to hear his proposal. " ' Miners ' means and includes prospectors as well as workers in or about mines, and all persons who are engaged or employed in or about any of the processes of mining as an industry, including surface operations, as by washing, hauling, assaying and milling as well as operations under ground."

I wish to propose an amendment to the amendment. Provision should be made so that men who are in un-

employment relief camps will not be deprived of their votes. It is very well known to everyone that men in the relief camps are more than twenty-five miles away from the place in which they are ordinarily registered and it is of little use to1 give them the right to the franchise unless you provide for their exercising it. I would move therefore that included among those who may vote by use of the absentee ballot there be added persons in any unemployment relief camp.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The section in regard to
relief camps has already been carried.
No.
Not for voting in relief camps.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In relief camps anyone Who is a miner or lumberman or sailor or fisherman can vote, I fancy, by the use of the absentee ballot, provided his home is in the province. It could not be taken in British Columbia for use in Halifax, for instance, and he has to be on the list where the vote is counted.

I am in sympathy with the purpose of this legislation but it is limited distinctly to four classes of people: fishermen, sailors, lumbermen and miners. These men are undoubtedly in many instances remote from ordinary polling places, but there is another class which is just as important and unfortunately to-day it is very numerous, that is, men engaged in relief camps. We have already recognized this class by making provision that they may be registered in their home districts, but these home districts are sometimes one hundred or two or three hundred miles from the camp in Which they are temporarily employed. It is all very well to make provision for their registration, but it is useless unless we give them an opportunity for voting, and there seems no reason why they should be discriminated against. It would be an easy matter for the minister to include as a fifth group those engaged in relief camps. We have already dealt with them in the other act. They are a clearly defined class, and I would ask the minister to add them to the list. It is bad enough for people to be out of work through no fault of their own, but it would be a serious matter if they were in practice disfranchised.

With all reserve of rights as to whether we will accept the whole amendment or not, which it is difficult to accept without consideration-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I read it for the purpose of making it public.

As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre very well eaid, we provide for the registration of men on unemployment relief; they are to be registered at the place from which they come before they enter the relief camps. There is no reason, if they are registered, why they should not poll their votes at the place at which they are when an election occurs. If we accept the principle and if it is found there are sufficient safeguards in the amendment as proposed by the minister, there is no reason why that category of person should not be added to the list of those who are to be included as voting as absentee voters.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is, provided they are on the list.
That applies to everybody in any case, lumbermen, sailors and everyone else.

With due reserve, I find the principle of this amendment unsound because a man has a right to vote in his constituency, in the area where he lives, and I do not see why a man should be permitted to vote within the province and outside the constituency in which he lives. This amendment has a strong smell of the War-time Elections Act. It .refers to fishermen, miners, sailors and lumbermen. If the ship of state docks at Riviere du Loup wharf with all its crew I am not afraid of it; we can take good care of it. But the principle is most unsound and it is absurd to give men the right to vote outside their constituency in order to fill the boxes with ballots of people who do not live in the constituency in which they vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not inclined to increase the list. In the last twenty-four hours I have heard many demands for increases for school teachers, ministers of the gospel, berry pickers and apple pickers. We have decided that this is a special privilege to the people to whom it has been given and it was in that light our committee discussed the matter.

I rise to say a word in defence of the old act of 1930. I feel that every citizen of this country, man or woman, who is a British subject and is over the age of twenty-one, should have the right to vote. The old act was not so bad. While this may be better, I cannot see that it is.

Mr. Speaker, may I call your attention to the fact that it is now twenty-five minutes to twelve. This house decided that it would adjourn at eleven o'clock. It seems to me that this is stretching the matter almost too far. Evidently we cannot complete this bill to-night.
Progress reported.
